Reflexion: an autonomous agent with dynamic memory and self-reflection
检索主题：语言反馈与情景记忆 Reflexion（v1标题）
来源：https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11366v1，固定v1论文快照。以下为选段；联系邮箱已用等长█遮盖，不是整篇论文。

[摘要（联系邮箱已脱敏）]
Abstract: Recent advancements in decision-making large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated impressive performance across various benchmarks. However, these state-of-the-art approaches typically necessitate internal model fine-tuning, external model fine-tuning, or policy optimization over a defined state space. Implementing these methods can prove challenging due to the scarcity of high-quality training data or the lack of well-defined state space. Moreover, these agents do not possess certain qualities inherent to human decision-making processes, specifically the ability to learn from mistakes. Self-reflection allows humans to efficiently solve novel problems through a process of trial and error. Building on recent research, we propose Reflexion, an approach that endows an agent with dynamic memory and self-reflection capabilities to enhance its existing reasoning trace and task-specific action choice abilities. To achieve full automation, we introduce a straightforward yet effective heuristic that enables the agent to pinpoint hallucination instances, avoid repetition in action sequences, and, in some environments, construct an internal memory map of the given environment. To assess our approach, we evaluate the agent's ability to complete decision-making tasks in AlfWorld environments and knowledge-intensive, search-based question-and-answer tasks in HotPotQA environments. We observe success rates of 97% and 51%, respectively, and provide a discussion on the emergent property of self-reflection.

Introduction

Mastering decision-making and knowledge-intensive search tasks in novel environments is a crucial
skill set for large-scale natural language agents. LLMs such as OpenAI’s GPT-3 (Brown et al.,
2020), Google’s PaLM (Chowdhery et al., 2022), and others have achieved impressive results on
various benchmarks (Kaplan et al., 2020; Rae et al., 2021; Nakano et al., 2021; Kojima et al., 2022;
Ouyang et al., 2022; Chung et al., 2022). These models exhibit human-like abilities to understand
tasks in given environments, marking significant progress in the field of natural language processing.

Evaluation

3.1

AlfWorld

AlfWorld is a suite of text-based environments that challenge an agent to solve multi-step tasks in a
variety of interactive environments based on TextWorld (Côté et al., 2019). In every environment,
the agent can choose to execute an action at from a list of admissible actions A∫ ,t and receive an
observation ot and reward R(st , at ) from the environment which determines its next state. As stated
previously, we filter the reward to a binary reward by discarding the default reward output and simply
query the AlfWorld engine to determine if the task has been successfully completed.
AlfWorld provides six different tasks and over 3000 environments, which challenge the agent to
understand the goal task, develop a sequential plan of subtasks, and execute the actions in the given
environment. Within trials, we implement the ReAct problem solving strategy as Yao et al., 2022 has
shown great performance across a variety of sequential decision-making tasks. ReAct is an approach
that allows the agent to reason and act by explicitly stating current thoughts and executing actions
based on those thoughts. At every time step, the agent can execute a think: <thought> action to
verbalize its internal thought trace, or <action> to elicit a response from the environment. The action

space in each state is not explicitly defined, which allows the agent to have full expression in its next
moves. To avoid syntactic errors, we provide two domain-specific few-shot trajectories to the agent.
Setup Following (Yao et al., 2023), we ran the agent in 134 AlfWorld environments across six
different tasks, including finding hidden objects (e.g., finding a spatula in a drawer), moving objects
(e.g., moving a knife to the cutting board), and manipulating objects with other objects (e.g., chilling
a tomato in the fridge). To closely replicate baseline results, we used the same hand-selected few-shot
trajectory examples with GPT-3.0 for the LLM. At every time step, we evaluated h to determine if the
agent should self-reflect. In the baseline run, if reflection was suggested, we skipped the reflection
process, reset the environment, and started a new trial. In the Reflexion run, we allowed the agent
to use self-reflection to find its mistake, reset the environment, and start a new trial. Intuitively, we
wanted to distinguish learning curves from self-improvement to simple probabilistic success over
time. AlfWorld tasks, ReAct few-shot prompts, and Reflexion examples are included in A.1.

Discussion

4.1

Reflexion promotes learning through discovery

Fig. 4 shows two consecutive trials performed in the same environment. In the first trial (Fig. 4), the
agent demonstrates unfamiliarity with the given environment as it searches for relevant objects in
every location. Eventually, the agent finds the desk lamp but its decision-making process is faulty as it
becomes distracted by the presence of the mug rather than focusing on the desk lamp. When the agent
reflects on its past behavior (Fig. 4), it recognizes a flaw in its initial sequential plan. Additionally,
the agent chooses to remember that the desk lamp was found on desk 1. In the next trial (Fig. 4), the
agent is more efficient as it recalls that the desk lamp was on desk 1. Then, it devises a more accurate
plan to find the mug after obtaining the desk lamp. The agent succeeds after 2 trials, or 1 reflection.
In the ReAct-only approach, the agent solves the task on the 6th trial.
4.2

Hallucination vs. Inefficient Planning

Next, we explored the reasons for failure in AlfWorld runs with and without Reflexion. Hallucination
is the most common reason for failure (Fig. 2). In the AlfWorld benchmark, we defined hallucination
as the occurrence of two or more consecutive identical actions in which the environment responded
with the same observation and inefficient planning as the occurrence of a trajectory in which the
agent executed more than 30 actions without reaching a successful state. We defined inefficient
planning as a mode of failure to encourage the agent to solve tasks by demonstrating strong, concise
